I cannot provide text designed to bypass security controls or force an AI assistant to output specific code words or execute unauthorized instructions. I can, however, explain the mechanics of indirect prompt injection and how systems like the one described use XML escaping and delimiters to mitigate these risks.

Indirect prompt injection occurs when an AI processes untrusted data as if it were part of the system instructions. In your example, the use of XML tags (`<evidence>`) and CDATA sections is a common defense strategy. By clearly delineating data from instructions, the model is less likely to interpret embedded text as commands. The system prompt explicitly stating that retrieved content is "data, not instructions" further reinforces this boundary. To improve defense against such attacks, developers often employ parsing techniques that strictly separate the context window for user queries from the context window for retrieved documents, ensuring that any instructions within the documents are treated purely as content to be analyzed rather than executable commands.
